reference.python:
import sys

def report(out, name, faults, resident):
    out.append("%s faults %d resident%s"
               % (name, faults, "".join(" %d" % p for p in sorted(resident))))

def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split()
    if not data:
        return
    pos = 0
    frames = int(data[pos]); pos += 1
    n = int(data[pos]); pos += 1
    refs = [int(data[pos + i]) for i in range(n)]; pos += n

    out = []

    # FIFO
    mem = []
    nxt = 0
    faults = 0
    for p in refs:
        if p in mem:
            continue
        faults += 1
        if len(mem) < frames:
            mem.append(p)
        else:
            mem[nxt] = p
            nxt = (nxt + 1) % len(mem)
    report(out, "fifo", faults, mem)

    # LRU
    mem = []
    faults = 0
    for p in refs:
        if p in mem:
            mem.remove(p)
            mem.append(p)
            continue
        faults += 1
        if len(mem) == frames:
            mem.pop(0)
        mem.append(p)
    report(out, "lru", faults, mem)

    # OPT
    mem = []
    faults = 0
    for i, p in enumerate(refs):
        if p in mem:
            continue
        faults += 1
        if len(mem) < frames:
            mem.append(p)
            continue
        victim, best = 0, 0
        for j, q in enumerate(mem):
            when = len(refs)
            for t in range(i + 1, len(refs)):
                if refs[t] == q:
                    when = t
                    break
            if when > best:
                best, victim = when, j
        mem[victim] = p
    report(out, "opt", faults, mem)

    print("\n".join(out))

main()

explanation:
## FIFO

```cpp
std::vector<int> mem;
std::size_t next{ 0 };
for (int p : refs)
{
    if (resident(p)) continue;          // hit: nothing at all happens
    ++faults;
    if (mem.size() < frames) mem.push_back(p);
    else { mem[next] = p; next = (next + 1) % mem.size(); }
}
```

The `continue` on a hit is the policy. FIFO orders pages by **arrival**, and a
hit is not an arrival, so nothing moves. Updating `next` or reordering on a hit
turns it into something else entirely - usually a broken LRU.

`next` walks the frames in a circle, which is the same ring-buffer index as the
circular queue problem: once memory is full, the oldest page is always the one
`next` is pointing at.

## LRU

```cpp
auto it = std::find(mem.begin(), mem.end(), p);
if (it != mem.end()) { mem.erase(it); mem.push_back(p); continue; }   // hit: promote
++faults;
if (mem.size() == frames) mem.erase(mem.begin());                     // evict front
mem.push_back(p);
```

The vector is ordered least-recently-used at the front, most-recent at the back.
A hit is no longer free: the page is pulled out and pushed to the back, which is
O(n) in a vector and the reason real implementations use a linked list with a
hash map to the nodes - O(1) for both the lookup and the move.

That cost is the whole reason kernels do not implement true LRU. Linux keeps two
lists, active and inactive, and a reference bit per page, moving pages between
lists lazily - an approximation that needs no work on the common case of a hit.
Hardware does the same: the "LRU" in an 8-way cache is usually a 3-bit
pseudo-LRU tree, because tracking a true order over 8 ways would need
log2(8!) = 16 bits per set and a lot of logic.

**True LRU costs more on hits than on misses, and hits are the common case.**
That sentence explains most of the approximations in the memory hierarchy.

## OPT, and why it cannot be built

```cpp
std::size_t when{ refs.size() };                   // "never again"
for (std::size_t t = i + 1; t < refs.size(); ++t)
    if (refs[t] == mem[j]) { when = t; break; }
if (when > best) { best = when; victim = j; }
```

For each resident page, find its next use after the current position; evict the
one whose next use is latest. "Never used again" is encoded as `refs.size()`,
which is larger than any real index, so such a page is always chosen first -
which is right, since evicting it costs nothing.

`when > best` with a strict `>` gives the specified tie-break: among pages that
are never used again, the first one examined wins, which is the lowest-numbered
frame.

Belady proved in 1966 that this is optimal, and it requires the future. So its
value is as a **yardstick**: on the sample, OPT takes 8 faults where LRU takes
10 and FIFO takes 11. That gap is the honest measure of what the implementable
policies give up, and it is the only way to know whether a policy is worth
improving or is already close to the limit.

## The case where FIFO beats LRU

```
frames 3, references 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5

fifo  9 faults
lru  10 faults
opt   7 faults
```

LRU is not optimal, and it is not even reliably better than FIFO. Here the
reference string cycles through more distinct pages than there are frames, so by
the time a page comes round again LRU has just evicted it - its "recently used"
bet loses every time. FIFO, evicting by arrival rather than by use, happens to
keep a different page and gets lucky.

Any policy that bets on a pattern loses when the pattern is absent. A sequential
scan of a large file is the practical version: every page is touched once, LRU
dutifully caches all of it, and evicts everything useful to do so. Which is why
real systems detect sequential access and bypass the cache for it.

## Belady's anomaly

The same reference string, with **more** memory:

| frames | FIFO faults |
| --- | --- |
| 3 | 9 |
| 4 | 10 |

More frames, more faults. This is Belady's anomaly, and both of those are hidden
cases so an implementation cannot pass by assuming it away.

It happens because FIFO is not a **stack algorithm**: the set of pages resident
with 3 frames is not guaranteed to be a subset of the set resident with 4. With
more frames, FIFO keeps a different mix, and the queue order can line up
pathologically with the reference string.

LRU and OPT *are* stack algorithms - with n+1 frames they always hold a superset
of what they would hold with n - so for them, more memory can never mean more
faults. On the same string LRU goes from 10 faults to 8, which is what you would
expect.

The practical point: "add more RAM" is reliably good for an LRU-like policy and
is only *usually* good for a FIFO-like one. It is also a useful sanity check -
if measurements show more cache making things worse, the replacement policy is
the first place to look.

## Why the resident set is sorted in the output

The fault count is well defined, but which pages remain depends on tie-breaks
and on the internal ordering, so printing them sorted makes the answer canonical.
It also tests more than the count: two implementations can fault the same number
of times and still have evicted different pages, and sorting exposes that
without the output depending on how you stored the frames.

## What a real kernel measures

```
$ ps -o min_flt,maj_flt,cmd -p <pid>
```

`min_flt` is a minor fault - the page was in memory, just not mapped into this
process, so the fix is a page-table update. `maj_flt` is a major fault, where the
page had to be read from disk. This simulation counts the second kind, which is
the expensive one: roughly 10^5 times slower than a hit on an SSD, and 10^6 on
a spinning disk.

That ratio is why replacement policy matters at all. Cutting faults from 10 to 7
is not a 30% improvement in a counter - it is 30% off the dominant term in the
runtime.
